author: ohtadmin
title: Dutch Harbor oyster farm OK'd
text:
An oyster farm in Dutch Harbor has been given unanimous approval to expand its operation by 45% despite two objections.
The application by Rocky Rhode Oyster Co. owner Brad Boehringer sought to expand his 3.5 acres from 7.8 to 11.3.
The Rhode Island Coastal Resources Management Council at a public hearing Jan. 13 gave its stamp of approval. Boehringer will use the added acreage to cultivate eastern oysters and bay scallops using low-profile floating baskets and bottom cages.
The reason for the expansion is “to improve commercial viability and longevity.”
“As our farm grows and takes on more demand from restaurants and wholesalers, we look toward a future where we can sell 1 million oysters a year, as well as provide our employees with year-round, stable employment,” the application said. “The expansion of this lease will allow us to reach that goal.”
Rocky Rhode is among six aquafarms covering 35 total acres in the harbor.
Sharon Purdie, of Westwind Drive, and Robert Jiao, of Seaside Drive, submitted letters against the application. Both mentioned trash along the shoreline.
“Debris from the farms remains on the beach,” Purdie wrote. “None of the debris has identification on it although it’s required. One piece is almost in front of our steps leading to the beach. Two other objects are on the south side of the creek and at least one is visible on the other side. Several items are farther down the beach closer to the farms.”
Jiao wrote that he bought his property “because of its beauty.” It’s “a shame,” however, to see such garbage on the shore.
“It’s as simple as being responsible enough to comb the bay, walk ashore and pick up stuff that is an eyesore and possible nautical hazard,” he said. “I can only imagine how much more detached oyster farm garbage will pile up with the proposed expansion.”
Purdie, aside from the garbage, also indicated concerns about the “notable increase in sand accumulation at the Great Creek entrance from Dutch Harbor.”
“Sand shoals are now extending out into the harbor, large quantities of sand are accumulating on the shores of the creek and one tidal pool is now completely closed off from water,” she wrote. “We have lived here for 20 years and have not seen this situation in the past. If this accumulation is allowed to continue, the creek will become landlocked, killing the marshes that are fed by it. Although it is unclear if this change is related to the oyster farms, the only change to this area of the harbor during this period has been the massive expansion of oyster farms and the gear used to anchor these to the floor of the harbor.”
